stem: When monitoring a pediatric solid-organ transplant recipient for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), which timing statement aligns with standard pediatric infection references?

options.text: PCP typically occurs after the first month following transplantation
PCP occurs only before the transplant operation
PCP never occurs when any immunosuppression is used
PCP is expected exclusively more than 2 years after every transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia typically occurs after the first month following transplantation, although trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis has essentially eliminated this problem when used.

rationale_incorrect.B: PCP is a post-transplant fungal pneumonia rather than a preoperative process.
rationale_incorrect.C: Immunosuppression increases PCP risk; prophylaxis prevents disease rather than immunosuppression preventing all risk without prophylaxis.
rationale_incorrect.D: Standard references describe typical onset after the first post-transplant month rather than exclusively after 2 years.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 17, Pediatric Infections → fungal → 1. PCP → a.–b.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Pneumocystis jirovecii … Typically occurs after the first month following transplantation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 17 → fungal infections → 1. PCP → b. (typically after first post-transplant month); PDF p. 943 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pediatric PCP timing angle distinct from TMP-SMX toxoplasma benefit (cctc-3068) and PCP discharge teaching (cctc-3042); anchor verified on Cupples p. 943.

stem: Which bacterial infection is described as the most common in pediatric renal transplant recipients per standard references?

options.text: Mediastinitis as the most common kidney transplant infection
Ascending cholangitis without any urinary involvement
Toxoplasmosis as the predominant early bacterial complication

explanation.rationale_correct: In pediatric renal transplant recipients, urinary tract infection—especially pyelonephritis with gram-negative organisms—is the most common bacterial infection.

rationale_incorrect.B: Mediastinitis is described among pediatric heart rather than kidney recipients.
rationale_incorrect.C: Ascending cholangitis is associated with pediatric liver transplantation rather than being the most common kidney infection.
rationale_incorrect.D: Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection rather than the most common bacterial complication in pediatric kidney recipients.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 17, Pediatric Infections → bacterial → 3.a. Renal transplant recipients → i.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Urinary tract infection, especially pyelonephritis, is the most common (gram-negative organisms)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 17 → bacterial infections → 3.a.i. (pediatric kidney UTI/pyelonephritis most common); PDF p. 943 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pediatric kidney bacterial-infection epidemiology distinct from adult asymptomatic bacteriuria (cctc-3012) and pediatric rejection presentation (cctc-3087); anchor verified on Cupples p. 943.

stem: A pediatric transplant recipient has a positive purified protein derivative (PPD) test before documented tuberculosis disease. Which post-transplant management step aligns with standard references?

options.text: Chest radiograph and isoniazid for at least 9 months post-transplant
No further evaluation because PPD positivity is ignored after transplant
Immediate isolated kidney transplantation without infectious assessment
Permanent discontinuation of all immunosuppression for 9 months

explanation.rationale_correct: Patients with tuberculosis history or positive PPD should have a chest x-ray and receive isoniazid for at least 9 months post-transplant.

rationale_incorrect.B: Positive PPD or TB history triggers chest imaging and isoniazid prophylaxis rather than being ignored.
rationale_incorrect.C: Infectious screening and prophylaxis are part of post-transplant management rather than bypassed.
rationale_incorrect.D: Isoniazid prophylaxis is added while immunosuppression continues per protocol rather than stopping all immunosuppression.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: positive purified protein derivative (PPD) test should have a chest x-ray and receive isoniazid for at least 9 months post transplant

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 17 → Tuberculosis → 2.b. (chest x-ray and isoniazid ≥9 months for PPD positivity); PDF p. 943 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pediatric TB/PPD prophylaxis angle distinct from community respiratory viruses (cctc-1056) and PCP timing (cctc-3093); anchor verified on Cupples p. 943.

stem: A coordinator is updating pediatric post-transplant bacterial infection teaching by organ type. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: In pediatric kidney recipients, urinary tract infection—especially pyelonephritis—is the most common bacterial infection.
In pediatric heart recipients, mediastinitis may occur with Staphylococcus aureus or gram-negative organisms.
In pediatric liver recipients, ascending cholangitis is associated with biliary tract abnormalities.
In pediatric lung recipients, bacterial pneumonia never involves Pseudomonas species.

explanation.rationale_correct: Pediatric kidney recipients most commonly develop UTI/pyelonephritis, heart recipients may develop mediastinitis with S. aureus or gram-negative organisms, and liver recipients may develop ascending cholangitis associated with biliary abnormalities. Pediatric lung pneumonia may involve Pseudomonas, so statement IV is false.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement III is also true—ascending cholangitis is associated with biliary tract abnormalities in pediatric liver recipients.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement IV is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement IV is false because Pseudomonas is among cited pediatric lung pneumonia pathogens.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: Urinary tract infection, especially pyelonephritis, is the most common … Mediastinitis (Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative organisms) … Ascending cholangitis associated with biliary tract abnormalities … pneumonia: Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 17 → bacterial infections → 3.a.–d. (organ-specific pediatric bacterial infection patterns); PDF p. 943 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Pediatric organ-specific bacterial-infection combo paired with UTI recall item (cctc-3094); anchor verified on Cupples p. 943.
